paragraphs.heading: A box that pumps heat out
paragraphs.text: A refrigerator, or fridge, is an appliance found in homes and businesses. It is an insulated compartment joined to a heat pump. That heat pump carries heat from inside the box out to the room, so the inside ends up colder than the air around it. The pump can be mechanical, electronic or chemical.

paragraphs.heading: Why cold keeps food
paragraphs.text: Refrigeration is a key way to store food all over the world. At low temperatures bacteria multiply more slowly, so food spoils more slowly too. A fridge holds its contents a few degrees above the point where water freezes, and perishable food keeps best between 3 and 5 °C. A freezer, whether a separate unit or part of a fridge, keeps its contents below freezing.

paragraphs.heading: How most fridges work
paragraphs.text: Most household fridges and freezers run on a vapor compression cycle. It is the same technology used in air conditioners. Artificial cooling itself began in 1755, when the Scottish professor William Cullen used a pump to make a partial vacuum above a container of diethyl ether. The ether boiled and soaked up heat from the air around it, and even made a little ice, though nothing practical came of it then.

paragraphs.heading: From experiment to industry
paragraphs.text: In 1805 the American inventor Oliver Evans described a closed vapor compression cycle for making ice. In 1834 Jacob Perkins, an American living in Britain, built the first working vapor compression system, a closed device that could run without stopping. The Scotsman James Harrison built the first practical one, and his 1856 patent covered systems using ether, alcohol or ammonia.

paragraphs.heading: Into the kitchen
paragraphs.text: Fridges for the home were invented in 1913, and in 1923 Frigidaire brought out the first self-contained unit. The arrival of Freon in the 1920s helped the market grow during the 1930s. Home freezers as separate compartments followed in 1940, and frozen food went from a luxury to an everyday item. Before all this, the icebox had been a common household appliance for almost 150 years.

paragraphs.heading: Cooling before electricity
paragraphs.text: People kept food cold long before any machine. Ancient Iranians built coolers called yakhchāls that relied on evaporative and radiative cooling. These had underground storage, a large, thickly insulated dome above ground, wind-catchers called badgirs and a series of aqueducts called qanats. In more recent times, before the electric fridge, icehouses and iceboxes packed with winter snow and ice kept food cool for most of the year.
